extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of science; philosophers of science; researchers learning scientific method and classification
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for how to recognise, classify, and respond to exceptional or anomalous phenomena in scientific investigation, and principles for forming and using classifications in scientific reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for known interfering causes before declaring law failure
rubrics_metrics.description: When a law of nature appears to fail because some other law has interfered with its action ... we have nothing to do but calculate as exactly as possible the amount of interference, and make allowance for it; the apparent failure of the law under examination should then disappear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigators should look for known physical/chemical/experimental causes that could alter outcomes (e.g., adhesive forces between glass and mercury, vapour films causing spheroidal ebullition, oxide films protecting iron) and quantitatively correct for them before concluding a law is violated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the possibility of previously undetected laws or forces
rubrics_metrics.description: A phenomenon which cannot be explained by any known laws may indicate the interference of undiscovered natural forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no known interfering cause explains an anomaly, treat the result as potential evidence of new laws (examples: loadstone magnetism leading beyond gravity; light–electricity relations in selenium). Such anomalies warrant further experimental inquiry rather than immediate dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule out accidental, secondary, or extraneous causes (domain-specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: The geologist must bear the possibility of interference in mind ... in archaeological investigations the greatest caution is requisite in allowing for secondary burials in ancient tombs and tumuli, for imitations, forgeries, casual coincidences, disturbance by subsequent races or by other archaeologists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field- and domain-specific sources of contamination, intrusion, or deception must be considered (e.g., transported fossils, later intrusive burials, forgeries). Exhaustively check context and provenance before treating a datum as an exception to a law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify exceptions to determine appropriate response
rubrics_metrics.description: When a law of nature appears to fail ... two cases may present themselves; the interfering law may be a known one, or it may have been previously undetected. The chapter also distinguishes limiting exceptions, real exceptions, unexplained anomalies, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sort anomalies into types (accidental/interference, limiting exceptions due to overgeneralisation, genuine contradictions requiring theory change, novel/unresolved phenomena) because each class prescribes a different response (adjust, restrict, reject, investigate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting exceptions: restrict the scope of overgeneralised laws
rubrics_metrics.description: It may happen that a law holding rigorously true of the facts actually under notice had been extended by generalisation to other series of facts then unexamined. Subsequent investigation may show the falsity of this generalisation, and the result must be to limit the law for the future to those objects of which it is really true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an anomaly shows that prior generalisation was too broad (examples: critical temperatures for liquefaction, limits to 'forced vibrations'), modify the stated domain of the law rather than abandoning its core for cases where it remains valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real exceptions: reject theories contradicted by conclusive experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: One single fact clearly irreconcilable with a theory involves its rejection ... If, then, by our senses we satisfy ourselves of the actual occurrence of the phenomena, the law must be rejected as illusory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an experimentally robust, replicated observation is genuinely incompatible with a law or theory, the correct response is to abandon or revise the theory; historical examples include refutation of Aristotelian 'nature abhors a vacuum' and Lavoisier's oxygen-as-acid-generator generalisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unresolved/unexplained anomalies are opportunities for discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: At every period of scientific progress there will exist a multitude of unexplained phenomena which ... are the outstanding facts upon which the labours of investigators must be exerted — the ore from which the gold of future discovery is to be extracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat persistent unexplained facts (e.g., anomalous vapour-densities, properties of sulphur/selenium) as promising leads; systematic investigation may group them into new principles or reveal relations to known laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use probabilistic (inverse) reasoning to weigh competing explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the principle of the inverse method of probability, the probability of any hypothetical explanation is affected by the probability of each other possible explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate extraordinary claims by comparing the likelihoods of alternative accounts (fraud, self-deception, experimental error, new phenomenon). Favor the explanation with higher comparative probability unless evidence strongly supports the extraordinary one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steer between credulity and scepticism — investigate strange reports rigorously
rubrics_metrics.description: When the discovery of new and peculiar phenomena conflicting with our theories ... is reported to us, it becomes no easy task to steer a philosophically correct course between credulity and scepticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not automatically accept strange claims nor reflexively dismiss them; require and seek clear evidence, repeatable observation, and careful controls before deciding. Be open to novelty but demand rigorous proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer mundane explanations (fraud, conjuring, self-deception) when probable
rubrics_metrics.description: It is on these grounds of probability that we should reject the so-called spiritualist stories ... The performances of conjurors sufficiently prove that it requires no very great skill to perform tricks the modus operandi of which shall entirely escape the notice of spectators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given frequent historical examples of fraud and deception, investigators should rigorously rule out trickery and cognitive biases before invoking new causes; demonstrate that mundane explanations are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about extending laws from limited observations
rubrics_metrics.description: So many gases have been reduced to the liquid state ... that scientific men rather hastily adopted the generalisation that all substances could exist in all three states. ... We must modify our previous views, and either assert that below a certain critical temperature every gas may be liquefied, or else assume that a highly condensed gas is, when above the critical temperature, indistinguishable from a liquid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid premature universal generalisations; check the limits of experiments and consider critical/limiting conditions before declaring universal applicability of a law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification is foundational to scientific reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification is the placing together, either in thought or in actual proximity of space, those objects between which identity has been detected. The value of classification is co-extensive with the value of science and general reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forming correct classes reduces multiplicity to unity, yields generalized knowledge, and enables substitutional reasoning (what is known of one member can apply to others insofar as identity holds). Use classification to organise inference and reduce complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of substitution within correctly formed classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Of every class, so far as it is correctly formed, the principle of substitution is true, and whatever we know of one object in a class we know of the other objects, so far as identity has been detected between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defining classes, explicitly state the identity conditions; only apply substitution-based inferences within those limits to avoid overextension and resultant anomalies.
